    AI Overview
    As of March 2026, the Biden administration's signature
    Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) plan is effectively terminated following court orders. Seven million+ borrowers must switch from SAVE to other, generally less generous, repayment plans (like the new Repayment Assistance Plan or standard plans) to avoid automatic reassignment and potentially higher monthly payments. 
    Key 2026 Updates (Post-SAVE Plan): 
    • The End of SAVE: The most generous income-driven repayment (IDR) plan, which offered 5% discretionary income payments and fast forgiveness, was killed by court rulings.
    • Borrower Action Needed: Borrowers have a 90-day window to switch to a legal plan.
    • New Alternatives: The Department of Education is introducing a "Repayment Assistance Plan" (with 30-year relief terms) and a Tiered Standard Plan.
    • Immediate Impacts: Failure to select a new plan could lead to being moved to the standard 10-year repayment plan, causing massive payment increases. 
    Background of the "Biden Plan" (Pre-2026 Litigation): 
    • 0% Interest: Covered unpaid monthly interest so balances did not grow.
    • Low Payments: Reduced monthly payments to $0 for low-income borrowers (under 225% of the poverty line) and 5% of discretionary income for undergraduates.
    • Forbearance: Enrolled borrowers were placed in interest-free forbearance while legal challenges occurred. 
    Current Status of Debt Forgiveness: 
    • Large-scale student debt cancellation initiatives have faced numerous legal roadblocks and were largely struck down by the Supreme Court in 2023.

    Trending posts and discussions
    The Trump administration is giving student loan borrowers enrolled in a Biden-era repayment plan an ultimatum: switch to another federal plan or automatically be placed in the most expensive one. There are more than 7 million people enrolled in the Saving on a Valuable Education plan, commonly known as Save, which offers lower monthly payments and a faster path to loan forgiveness than other income-driven repayment plans. Nearly half of those borrowers have incomes that are low enough to qualify for zero-dollar monthly payments. If they fail to switch programs, their loans will be moved to the standard plan with fixed payments over 10 years, which could lead to whopping increases in their monthly bills. On Friday, the Education Department is set to begin emailing Save borrowers to encourage them to apply to a different repayment plan.
